intro: Luke Faulkner plays the Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2, marked Larghetto. The F♯-major melody becomes more and more ornamented, a quick middle section in murmuring figuration follows, and when the opening returns it carries new ornaments.

sections.label: A · Song with curling ornaments
sections.mNote: The right hand sings above widely spaced bass and chords

sections.label: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
sections.mNote: Dotted rhythms over quick inner notes and a leaping bass

sections.label: A′ · The ornamented song returns
sections.mNote: The opening melody comes back with new flourishes

cues.title: Opening melody, upbeat and bars 1–2
cues.text: The melody begins with an upbeat from A♯ to B, then falls through the notes of a C♯ chord. The left hand holds a low C♯ in bar 1 and moves to F♯ in bar 2.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–2: A♯–B upbeat, C♯ bass in bar 1, F♯ bass in bar 2. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Ferdinand Hiller
cues.text: Chopin dedicated the three nocturnes of Op. 15, published in 1833–34, to the German pianist Ferdinand Hiller. In a joint letter to Hiller of 20 June 1833 he wrote that Liszt was at that moment playing his études, “transporting me outside of my respectable thoughts”.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, Nocturnes, Op. 15: composed 1830–33, first published 1833–34, dedicated to Ferdinand Hiller: https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes,_Op.15_(Chopin,_Frédéric). Chopin, Liszt and Franchomme to Hiller, Paris, 20 June 1833, letter 76 in Chopin’s Letters, coll. Henryk Opienski, trans. E. L. Voynich (New York: Knopf, 1931), pp. 170–71: https://archive.org/details/chopinsletters00chop

cues.title: Counter-theme in F♯ minor
cues.text: A second theme in F♯ minor follows the opening melody. Its phrases rise into the upper register, then descend in short runs marked dolcissimo, very sweetly. The bass keeps moving under the long upper notes.
cues.evidence: Mieczysław Tomaszewski identifies the F♯-minor counter-theme and its rising and falling phrases: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173. Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 17–24: https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Doppio movimento, bars 25–32
cues.text: At bar 25 the tempo doubles (doppio movimento), and the piano stays sotto voce. In the same hand a dotted melody sounds above quick notes, while the bass leaps below.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32, marked doppio movimento and sotto voce. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the Larghetto theme
cues.text: At bars 47–52 the quick figures slow, molto rallentando and smorzando, and move down towards the middle of the keyboard. After a pause, a Tempo, the opening A♯–B turn returns. The Larghetto melody is repeated with added ornaments in small notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52: molto rallentando, smorzando, a pause, a Tempo and the ornamented reprise. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Luke Faulkner’s training
cues.text: Faulkner studied piano and composition at Chetham’s, then music at Oxford, then screen composition at Edinburgh. He graduated from Edinburgh in 2014, having studied recording and engineering as well as writing music for film.
cues.evidence: Luke Faulkner’s own biography gives his studies at Chetham’s, Oxford and Edinburgh, including the 2014 screen-composition degree: https://www.lukefaulkner.com/about

transitions.title: Dominant seventh on C♯ at doppio movimento
transitions.to: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
transitions.how: The slow section ends on repeated A♯s. The bass then moves to C♯, with E♯, G♯ and B above it, which makes a dominant seventh. Chopin marks the new passage doppio movimento and sotto voce. The right hand now plays a dotted tune with quick notes beneath it, and the left hand makes wide jumps.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 24–26. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

transitions.title: A pause, then A♯–B
transitions.from: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
transitions.how: Over a low C♯ the repeated figures slow and die away, marked molto rallentando, smorzando. The bass stops, and a pause separates the last figure from the A♯–B upbeat of the opening. Marked a Tempo, the melody returns over C♯ and reaches the F♯ in the bass in the following bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–50. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
